extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, potential petitioners (challengers), and patent owners considering or litigating IPRs
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and strategic guidance for filing, defending, and evaluating Inter Partes Review (IPR) proceedings before the USPTO PTAB, including institution standards, timing, estoppel, discovery limits, and comparative advantages versus district-court litigation. Useful for attorneys and parties deciding whether to pursue or defend an IPR and how to structure petitions/responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review (grounds and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR is a trial proceeding conducted at the PTAB to review patentability of one or more claims in a patent only on a ground that could be raised under §§ 102 or 103, and only on the basis of patents and printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR cannot be used to raise other statutory grounds (e.g., §101, §112) or rely on evidence other than patents and printed publications. Petitioners should craft grounds limited to novelty and obviousness and cite patents/printed publications as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible petitioners (who can file)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party (that is not estopped) other than the patent owner can file an IPR petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for prior actions that cause estoppel before filing. Owners cannot file to challenge their own patents; third parties, competitors, and other challengers may file subject to estoppel rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-filing estoppel triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel triggers: Service of complaint alleging infringement >1 year earlier; Final written decision in a previous IPR/PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner who was served with an infringement complaint more than one year earlier may be barred from filing an IPR. Prior final written decisions from PTAB can also trigger estoppel. Assess timing and prior proceedings carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: availability and filing deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR available starting 9 months after grant (if no PGR was filed); 1-year time limit from service of infringement complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a Post-Grant Review (PGR) was filed, IPR availability is affected. Parties should calendar the 9-month post-grant window and the 1-year bar from an infringement complaint when planning options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard (threshold for instituting review)
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR may be instituted upon showing: "There is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one claim challenged."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the PTAB's threshold for institution and is slightly higher than the "substantial new question" standard of ex parte reexamination. Petitioners must present sufficient prior art and argument to meet the reasonable-likelihood standard for at least one claim. Institution decisions are generally final and not appealable at that stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure phases and statutory timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: 1. Petition Phase (3 months) — Petitioner files IPR petition; Patent owner has 3 months to file Preliminary Response (optional). 2. Institution Decision (6 months from filing) — PTAB decides whether to institute. 3. Trial Phase (12 months from institution) — Patent owner Response (3 months), Petitioner Reply, Patent owner Surreply, Oral Hearing, Final Written Decision. 4. Appeal — Federal Circuit appeal available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutory timelines strictly. Institution decisions are made within ~6 months of filing; final written decisions generally within 12 months of institution (with some extensions). Prepare for each phase in advance (e.g., evidence, declarations, motions, hearing preparation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited discovery available: Initial mandatory disclosures; Routine discovery (cited references, supplemental information); Additional discovery (only if "in the interests of justice"); Depositions of declarants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery in IPRs is much narrower than in district court litigation. Parties should target narrow, PTAB-appropriate discovery (e.g., prior-art references, core factual support) and be prepared to justify requests for additional discovery under the "interests of justice" standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard of review in IPR: preponderance of evidence (district court: clear and convincing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PTAB uses preponderance of the evidence for unpatentability, it is a lower burden for petitioners than district-court litigation. This difference is a key factor when deciding whether to challenge a patent via IPR vs. district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effects after final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: After final written decision, petitioner is estopped from raising in: USPTO proceedings, District court litigation, ITC investigations. Estoppel applies to any ground "raised or reasonably could have been raised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel is strict and a major strategic consideration. Petitioners must evaluate which grounds are included in the petition and what could reasonably have been raised to avoid being barred from later asserting those grounds in other forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-party IPRs and joinder (35 U.S.C. §315(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Joinder allowed under 35 USC 315(c): Multiple petitioners can join an existing IPR; Common after one party files first; Reduces costs across parties; Avoids estoppel for joining party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder can be a cost-sharing and defensive strategy. Joining later does not necessarily subject the joining party to the same estoppel as the original petitioner—consider timing and the PTAB's joinder practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director discretion and Fintiv factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent trend: USPTO Director discretion to deny institution (Fintiv factors); Parallel litigation considerations; Sovereign immunity defenses; Stays of district court litigation pending IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director may exercise discretion to deny institution based on factors (commonly referenced as Fintiv factors) related to parallel district-court litigation. Petitioners and owners should analyze parallel proceedings and timing when assessing institution risk and strategies for stays or motions to stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations for filing an IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare prior art that wasn't considered during prosecution; Consider whether claims you'd amend are problematic; Evaluate parallel litigation timing; Budget for 1-year+ proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful petitions often present strong, unconsidered prior art and tailor arguments to the PTAB's institution standard. Budget and timing (including potential coordination with district-court cases) are essential. Consider the amendment prospects and estoppel consequences before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations for defending against an IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary Response is critical (early dismissal possible); Argue strong patent owner interests; Use Director discretionary denial factors; Amend claims if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a persuasive Preliminary Response can sometimes prevent institution. Defendants (patent owners) should highlight patent-strength factors, attack the petition's sufficiency under the reasonable-likelihood standard, and consider claim amendments or other motions to preserve claim scope and value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of IPR as a forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages of IPR: 1. Faster: 18 months or less from filing to final disposition. 2. Cheaper than litigation: Limited discovery. 3. Higher invalidation rates: ~75% of instituted IPRs result in some claims being invalidated. 4. Specialized adjudicators: PTAB judges have technical backgrounds. 5. Standard of review: Preponderance of evidence (district court: clear and convincing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These comparative advantages inform the decision to pursue IPR. Weigh speed, cost, and the PTAB's experience against estoppel risks and scope limitations when choosing between IPR and district-court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal route
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit appeal available from final written decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can appeal PTAB final written decisions to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Consider appellate strategy and prerequisites (e.g., issue preservation) during the IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison: IPR vs. district-court litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many parties pursue both: IPR can stay district court litigation; Different burden of proof (preponderance vs. clear and convincing); IPR limited to specific grounds; Litigation broader; Settlement options different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tradeoffs: IPR offers a faster, lower-burden, narrower forum limited to §§102/103 based on patents/printed publications, while district court offers broader remedies and discovery but requires a higher proof standard. Coordination and parallel-proceeding strategy are common.
